blocks.text: Folding of filter paper is important and is done in two ways.

items: Filtration by a glass funnel and filter paper is usually a slow process. As the mixture is poured onto the filter paper, the solvent (water) passes through leaving behind the suspended particles on the filter paper. Filter papers are available in a variety of porosities (pore sizes). Which pore size is to be used, depends upon the size of particles in the precipitate. The filter paper should be large enough so that it is one-fourth to one-half full of precipitate at the end of filtration. In this way, the filtrate runs down the side of beaker without splashing. A complete filtration assembly is shown in Figure 15.1.

blocks.alt: Three drawings: a round filter paper with a dashed line down the middle (first fold), the half circle with a dashed line across it (second fold), and the paper opened into a cone (forming the cone).
blocks.caption: Figure 15.2a: Folding of filtration paper (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.2a).

blocks.text: The folded filter paper may then be inserted into 60-degree funnel, moistened with water and firmly pressed down.

items: The rate of filtration through conical funnel can be considerably increased using a Fluted Filter Paper, for preparation of such a paper ordinary filter paper in folded in such a way that a fan like arrangement with alternate elevations and depressions at various folds is obtained Fig (15.2 b).

blocks.alt: Seven steps: filter disk; fold in half; fold in half again; fold to crease the quarter section; fold to crease the eight section; the pleated accordion shape; open filter cone.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.2b: Fluted filter paper (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.2b).

blocks.text: After filtration, the liquid which is obtained in the conical flask underneath the funnel is called the filtrate. The sand left behind on the funnel is called the residue.
